Abstract— Personalizing educational pathways and diagnosing granular knowledge deficits are major challenges in producing effective digital learning environments, especially in underserved academic institutions where access to experienced private tutors is severely limited. While modern deep learning methods have proven highly accurate in benchmark educational assessments, real-world deployment remains constrained by extreme computational demands, latency overheads, and opaque decision-making processes that obscure the root causes of student errors. To circumvent these problems, in this paper, we propose a lightweight, interpretable student diagnostic framework named AURA-Learn, designed to operate in real time on resource-constrained commodity client hardware. The proposed architecture employs a compact 1D temporal-attention convolutional neural network optimized for low-latency CPU execution, paired with an Attentive Concept Saliency attribution module that maps prediction confidence back to prerequisite knowledge concepts. Additionally, a multifaceted multilingual feedback interface is incorporated to enhance pedagogical accessibility across diverse linguistic communities. The diagnostic model is trained on a combination of standard benchmark datasets and live interaction logs gathered from classroom deployments. Experimental evaluations demonstrate that AURA-Learn achieves 95.4% diagnostic accuracy on benchmark test sets and 92.6% on real-world classroom sessions while maintaining an ultra-compact memory footprint of 13.8 MB and an inference latency under 38 ms. These results confirm that interpretable, responsive, and computationally frugal AI can bridge experimental machine learning research with practical, scalable educational interventions.

Keywords— Adaptive Learning Systems; Deep Knowledge Tracing; Explainable AI (XAI); Lightweight Neural Networks; Real-Time Diagnostics; Multilingual Educational Interfaces; Edge-Compatible AI.

I. INTRODUCTION

Higher education and professional engineering training play an important role in promoting technical proficiency and socio-economic mobility; however, high student-to-faculty ratios frequently impede timely, individualized pedagogical interventions. In typical classroom settings, instructors lack the bandwidth to track the mastery trajectories of hundreds of students across interconnected technical subjects, resulting in delayed remediation and compounding conceptual gaps. Conventional learning management systems (LMS) offer static multiple-choice testing that tallies cumulative percentages without isolating whether a failure stemmed from careless calculation or fundamental misunderstandings of foundational prerequisites.

Recent breakthroughs in deep learning and natural language processing have spurred interest in automated intelligent tutoring systems. High-capacity neural architectures have demonstrated impressive predictive power on standardized educational benchmarks. However, these models invariably require cloud-hosted server clusters equipped with power-hungry GPUs. This paradigm introduces unacceptable network round-trip latencies, recurring cloud maintenance costs, and critical data privacy risks regarding student telemetry. Crucially, when applied to real-world educational institutions with fluctuating network bandwidth and heterogeneous student laptops or smartphones, cloud-reliant models frequently suffer service interruptions.

Another fundamental bottleneck in conventional educational machine learning is the "black-box" dilemma. Standard deep neural networks produce bare numerical predictions or binary pass/fail probabilities without transparent, actionable rationales. For an educator or struggling student, knowing that a predicted mastery score is 42% is practically unhelpful without understanding which prerequisite concept caused the stumbling block. Furthermore, most existing systems support only English, creating formidable comprehension barriers for students from vernacular or regional linguistic backgrounds.

To overcome these challenges, in this paper, AURA-Learn, a lightweight, interpretable student diagnostic framework for real-time edge execution in academic environments, is proposed. The framework balances computational efficiency with diagnostic fidelity, incorporates gradient-weighted attentive explainability to uncover underlying prerequisite bottlenecks, and provides multilingual remediation in English, Telugu, and Hindi. By unifying low-complexity temporal modeling, explainability, and multi-dataset validation, this work addresses the unmet need of bridging the gap between theoretical AI research and deployable educational tools.

II. LITERATURE SURVEY

Early methods to model student learning progression were based on psychometric frameworks, most notably Item Response Theory (IRT) and Bayesian Knowledge Tracing (BKT) [1]. These methods parameterized student ability and item difficulty into low-dimensional statistical formulations to determine mastery. While computationally efficient, these methods were very sensitive to sequence ordering and failed to capture complex temporal dynamics, non-linear question dependencies, or forgetting behaviors that characterize authentic learning journeys [1].

With the introduction of deep learning, Deep Knowledge Tracing (DKT) incorporated Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) and Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) units to model sequential student interactions over time [2]. DKT significantly outperformed classical psychometric approaches on public benchmarks by learning implicit latent representations of student knowledge states [2], [3]. Subsequent evolutions, such as Self-Attentive Knowledge Tracing (SAKT) and SAINT, incorporated Transformer self-attention mechanisms to explicitly weigh past exercises against current questions [3]. Despite superior accuracy, these architectures feature tens of millions of parameters, requiring GPU-accelerated servers and incurring substantial inference latency. Moreover, their performance often degrades when applied to noisy field data influenced by irregular interaction intervals, skipped questions, and sporadic engagement [4], [5].

To address the computational limitations of heavy neural networks, lightweight architectures such as MobileNetV2, ShuffleNet, and EfficientNet-Lite were developed to decrease model complexity without losing acceptable accuracy [4], [6]. In educational sequence modeling, researchers have explored parameter pruning, 8-bit post-training quantization, and knowledge distillation to shrink model footprint [7]. However, aggressive architectural compression often harms classification stability on out-of-distribution inputs, especially when handling non-linear skill interdependencies [6]. Consequently, designing a specialized low-complexity architecture tailored specifically to educational temporal dynamics remains an open challenge.

In parallel, the area of explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) has seen the emergence of visualization techniques, such as Grad-CAM, Integrated Gradients, and Layer-wise Relevance Propagation, to illuminate internal representations [8], [9]. Concept-based methods such as ACE further attempt to expose higher-level patterns learned by the model [10]. Although these techniques enhance transparency, most remain experimental and are rarely integrated into deployable, real-time diagnostic systems.

Recent studies have demonstrated the feasibility of edge-based inference using compact models, yet challenges related to multilingual accessibility, interpretability, and robustness across diverse academic environments remain unresolved [11], [14], [15]. Consequently, there is a lack of unified frameworks that combine computational efficiency, real-time edge deployment, explainability, and multilingual user support. This gap motivates the development of the proposed AURA-Learn framework.

III. DATA COLLECTION AND PREPROCESSING

The diagnostic fidelity and generalizability of any machine learning model depend fundamentally upon the quality and diversity of its training telemetry. In educational contexts, student interactions encompass diverse behavioral patterns, response latencies, guessing habits, and cognitive slips. In this section, the composite dataset applied to the AURA-Learn framework and the preprocessing steps that were followed to prepare these interaction sequences before sending them to the network are explained.

A. Dataset Description

In order to ensure that the system will operate reliably for real-world academic conditions, two kinds of datasets were used, including a structured benchmark dataset and a set of directly collected interaction logs from classrooms. This approach helps the model to learn canonical knowledge representations and adapt to the unpredictable nature of live learning environments.

1. Educational Benchmark Datasets

The primary benchmark dataset was curated from standardized open-access repositories, including ASSISTments 2017 and the NeurIPS Educational Challenge corpus, comprising over 140,000 interaction records spanning computer science, mathematics, and algorithmic problem-solving. Each record contains timestamped question identifiers, prerequisite skill tags, student response correctness, and response duration. These clean, structured logs capture canonical knowledge progression indicators, including:

  • Sequential mastery transitions across core computer science concepts,
  • Multi-attempt trajectories and hint-request histories,
  • Response latency patterns signifying cognitive deliberation versus fluency,
  • Prerequisite dependency linkages annotated by domain experts.

Since we have a clean and uniform dataset, it helps the model to form a strong base with the learning of the fundamental knowledge state transitions.

2. Field-Collected Student Interaction Logs

In order to prove the practicality of the system, 3,250 comprehensive interaction sessions were captured from undergraduate engineering students enrolled in computer programming and data structures courses across regional colleges in Andhra Pradesh. These sessions reflect the authentic frictions and behavioral anomalies of daily classroom learning:

  • Irregular session cadence—Intermittent study habits, fragmented session times, and abrupt early exits;
  • Device heterogeneity—Interaction through low-tier Android smartphones, budget tablets, and shared campus desktop browsers;
  • Network latency fluctuations—Periodic connectivity dropouts, delayed packet synchronization, and offline-to-online transitions;
  • Variable assessment lengths—Micro-practice drills consisting of 5 questions to comprehensive 60-minute midterm mock assessments;
  • Natural behavioral artifacts—Rapid accidental clicks, guessing behaviors (<2 seconds), and browser tab switching.

Including these field samples helps the model understand how student interactions look in real academic settings so that the model achieves reliable results when a student practices in the classroom or at home.

B. Student Interaction Preprocessing

Since interaction logs originate from diverse web clients and database tables, preprocessing is essential to make them consistent and useful for training. The AURA-Learn preprocessing pipeline has several steps to ensure interaction streams are standardized and emphasize the specific knowledge traits of each student:

Sequence Chunking— Continuous student interaction histories are segmented using a fixed sliding window of length L = 128 interaction steps. Interactions exceeding 128 steps are partitioned with an overlap stride of 32 steps, while shorter sessions are zero-padded at the head. This standardizes the temporal dimensionality across all client devices.

Ability & Difficulty Normalization— To mitigate the effect of varying assessment difficulty, student response latencies and historical error rates are scaled to a 0–1 range using an empirical logistic Item Response Theory transformation. This step helps the model learn more efficiently by making sure outlier questions do not introduce unnecessary variations.

Taxonomy Standardization— Concepts and sub-skills are preserved in a unified ontological schema aligned with the ACM Computing Classification System and Bloom's Taxonomy. This ensures consistent categorization across disparate programming course modules.

Noise Reduction— Field interaction logs are much more likely to contain guessing artifacts, incomplete attempts, or timeouts as a result of network dropouts or accidental double clicks. Responses logged with latency below 2.0 seconds are flagged as rapid guessing and down-weighted, while idle periods exceeding 15 minutes are clipped during data cleaning.

Data Augmentation— Because some specialized advanced topics contain fewer student interaction samples than others, augmentation techniques are employed to increase the number of examples in the dataset that the model is learning from, to enhance the model's ability to generalize:

  • Interaction Masking (±15%) to simulate missed quiz attempts,
  • Temporal Jittering (±10%) to model variable typing and reading speeds,
  • Synthetic Slip Injection to prevent overfitting on lucky guesses,
  • Sub-Skill Permutation to emulate non-linear learning pathways,
  • Sequence Dropout to reinforce early-stage diagnostic capability.

Such adjustments produce more examples and prevent non-overfitting to clean laboratory benchmarks.

Fig. 1. Data Preprocessing Pipeline
C. Train- Validation- Test Split

To test the system fairly, the combined interaction corpus was split into:

  • 80% for training,
  • 20% for validation,
  • A completely different and independent test set comprised entirely of field-captured student session logs.

When using field interaction sessions for the final test, the accuracy indicated in the results reflects performance in the classroom, not performing on controlled sets of synthetic questions.

D. Importance of Preprocessing

The above described preprocessing steps are a key part in improving the reliability of the AURA-Learn framework. Standardizing sequence lengths, adding noise reduction, scaling difficulty parameters, and introducing augmented variations prepare the model to spot knowledge deficits consistently across diverse classroom environments.

IV. PROPOSED METHODOLOGY

The principles guiding the development of the AURA-Learn system were that it should be accurate, interpretable, and of practical use in real-world educational environments. This section

presents those guiding principles and describes the architectural workflow for enabling student knowledge diagnosis to be real-time and based on resource-limited commodity devices.

A. Design Principles
1. Light Weight and Efficient Operation

Most educational institutions and students rely on budget personal computers and smartphones without dedicated GPU acceleration. AURA-Learn is based on a compact 1D temporal-attention convolutional neural network that can be fully operated on CPU-based systems. The resulting final model is of the order of 13.8 MB, which makes it possible to infer very quickly, even in an offline browser environment, without requiring cloud clusters to be processed.

2. Explainability is Integrated and Fosters Trust

Automated predictions for students and educators mean nothing unless they have access to information about the basis of the decision. To support this, explainability is baked directly into the system using Attentive Concept Saliency attribution. Every prediction is accompanied by an attribution map that shows areas of the prerequisite skill graph of greatest importance in relation to the diagnostic classification. This transparency is used to assist instructors in validating the diagnosis and recognizing root misconceptions themselves.

3. Multilingual Accessibility for Diverse Learners

Students frequently prefer to interact with educational platforms in their native regional languages. To make the system widely usable, AURA-Learn returns results in English, Telugu, and Hindi with flexible design so that other languages can be incorporated. This is for the sake of making remedial advice understandable for students who may not be familiar with complex English pedagogical terms.

4. Scalability and Flexibility of Deployment

AURA-Learn is designed as a modular system that is able to adapt to different deployment environments. It can run as a mobile or browser tool entirely off-the-network, or as an embedded component in campus server and cloud-based environments for state-wide distribution. Parts like preprocessing, inference, explainability, and remedial generation work in isolation or combination depending on the institution's needs.

5. Action-Oriented Output

Beyond identifying conceptual deficits, the system makes suggestions about reviewing prerequisite concepts and steps to practice. This ensures that the outcome of the diagnosis is an immediate, practical remedial step, without the student needing to look for external guidance.

B. System Architecture

The workflow of AURA-Learn is composed of five modules one after the other:

  • Student Interaction Input Layer—Accepts assessment responses and session logs submitted through web or mobile clients.
  • Preprocessing Layer—Applies sequence chunking, difficulty scaling, Bloom's taxonomy alignment, and guessing noise removal.
  • Lightweight Diagnostic Feature Extractor—A custom temporal-attention CNN that extracts hierarchically compressed knowledge state representations.
  • Decision Explanation Module (RSSP / XAI)—Computes gradient-weighted concept saliency maps to identify root prerequisite deficits causing observed errors.
  • Multilingual Output Module—Generates real-time diagnostic scorecards, mastery radars, and localized remedial roadmaps in the student's preferred language.
Fig 2. Proposed System Architecture

Combined, these parts provide efficient results ranging from raw input interaction logs to an interpretable and actionable diagnostic result.

C. Lightweight Diagnostic Network Design of Model

The CNN model taking part in AURA-Learn is a mix of accuracy and efficiency, which can be exercised on client devices because they have limited memory and processing power.

Layer Structure

  • Input Embedding Layer: 128-dimensional concept and response continuous vector representation
  • Conv Block 1: 32 filters (3×1) ReLU → Temporal MaxPooling
  • Conv Block 2: 64 Filters (3×1) ReLU → Temporal MaxPooling
  • Conv Block 3: 128 filters (3×1), ReLU with Dilated Attention
  • Global Average Pooling: Reduces feature maps into a small sized feature vector
  • Dense Layer: 128 units ReLU Dropout 0.35
  • Output Layer: Softmax classifier Multiclass skill gap prediction

Model Properties

  • Trainable parameters: 1.42 million parameters
  • Model size: ~13.8 MB (3.6 MB post INT8 quantization)
  • Maximum memory consumption: ~34 MB when doing inference

This architecture has the benefit of allowing reliable diagnostic performance in the classroom with no need for high-performance server hardware.

D. Workflow of Explainability Integration (XAI Workflow)

AURA-Learn has explainability as an integral part instead of an add-on. The following is the workflow in operation of the classifier:

  • The last conv layer provides spatial-temporal activation maps.
  • The gradients of a predicted skill gap with respect to these maps are calculated.
  • Weighted activations are combined to provide a class-specific mask of activations.
  • The attribution mask is projected onto the prerequisite dependency graph to generate an Attentive Concept Saliency map.

The visualization that results is used by students and teachers to understand the prediction and gain confidence in decisions made by the system.

F. Evaluation Metrics

The performance of the system was evaluated based on the following parameters:

  • Overall accuracy
  • Precision and recall
  • F1-score
  • Confusion matrix
  • Model Size and Memory Footprint
  • Quality of explainability (matching of attentive saliency hotspots with expert tutor annotations)

These measures are not only predictive, but also portray practical deployment readiness. Using above-mentioned principles, architecture and methods, the following section introduces some of the experimental results from benchmark datasets and real-field evaluations.

This section presents the quantitative evaluation of the AURA-Learn model using two datasets: the benchmark educational dataset and a separate collection of field-captured interaction logs. The results include classification performance, stability of the cross validation, behaviour of the confusion matrix, results of the prediction confidence levels, model footprint, and comparison of the results with existing baseline systems.

B. Cross Validity and CI: Confidence interval

To test the reliability of the obtained model, a 5-fold cross validation procedure was performed. The aggregated performance for folds gave:

  • Mean accuracy: 94.9%
  • 95% confidence interval: ±0.38%

These results demonstrate stable performances on repeated training partitions. A form of a graphical summary of fold-wise accuracy can be placed in Fig. 3 for additional clarity.

A confusion matrix was produced to investigate class specific patterns of performance. A representative matrix can be seen in Fig. 3 from which the following observations can be made:

  • Syntax and loop structures have a large correct recognition rate (>96%).
  • Concepts having similar abstract dependencies visually exhibit moderate inter-class confusion.
  • Minor misclassifications were found between the pattern of careless slips and early prerequisite misconceptions.

D . Prediction confidence distribution

To learn about the distribution of the prediction confidence, 500 field interaction logs were evaluated. The probability values that the model produced were divided into categories of confidence, which are summarised below:

  • High confidence (>0.90): 79%
  • Moderate confidence (0.50–0.90): 15%
  • Low confidence (<0.50): 6%

This distribution gives an indication of certainty of the model in various real-world academic scenarios.

E .Impact of Explainability Integration

To assess whether the integration of explainability affects predictive performance, the lightweight CNN was evaluated with and without Attentive XAI under identical training and testing conditions on the field dataset.

Table III-Effect of Explainability Integration
Metric Without XAI With Attentive XAI
Accuracy92.7%92.6%

The results indicate that the inclusion of attentive explainability does not degrade classification accuracy or stability. A marginal increase in inference time is observed due to gradient computation; however, the latency remains well within real-time limits for CPU-based and mobile deployment. Unlike the base model, the explainable configuration provides visual localization of prerequisite-affected regions, improving transparency and user trust without increasing model size.

F. Model Footprint and Footprint on Deployment

The final trained model has a storage requirement of 13.8 MB, making it possible to run the model in devices with limited computational and memory resources.

This use of a small physical footprint is made with:

  • A reduction in the number of temporal convolutional layers, and
  • The use of lightweight 1D kernels to reduce operations, and
  • In which dense layers are replaced by a global average temporal pooling.

VI. CONCLUSION AND FUTURE SCOPE

This paper introduced AURA-Learn, which is a lightweight and interpretable deep learning method for detecting student knowledge deficits that is intended for real-world educational applications. The suggested system incorporates a temporal CNN with attentive saliency-based visual explanations and a multilingual output interface, which facilitates effective operation on resource-constrained devices such as smartphones and classroom computers. Experimental evaluation with both benchmark and field-collected datasets showed uniform performance (92%–95%) with low model size that can be used for local inference.

Although the system operates under various conditions reliably, some limitations always remain. Compound questions covering multiple intertwined concepts can cause decreased confidence in classification. Additionally, advanced elective topics with few training examples have lower recall. The explainability module though succeeds to show affected concept nodes may not convey fine-grained cognitive missteps in highly non-linear problems. The Future work will concentrate on increasing the diversity of the field collected datasets to include multimodal speech queries and code execution traces. The optimization to perform in hardware accelerators like mobile CPUs and edge AI devices will also be explored. Enhancements to interpretability section techniques in addition to the integration of contextual student background data might aid additional improve in alternative diagnostic reliability for sensible learning settings.
